Hi, Renato. Let us do the weekly status update. Are the Porto Alegre clinics on track?
Mostly, yes. The highlight: we did the joint visit on Tuesday, and Doctor Costa said she was happy to see us again.
That is good news. Did she say she would come back to us?
Not yet. She told us she needed a month to finish her stock from the competitor. So that clinic is a little behind schedule.
Okay. Is there a blocker I should know about?
Yes, I want to flag one. The distributor told me the November shipment would arrive two weeks late.
Two weeks? That could hurt us again. Who is the action item on?
It is on me. I will call the supply team today, and I will report back by Friday.
Perfect. And the second clinic?
That one is on track. The owner said they had a training day the following week, and he invited our consultant.
Great. Send me the next steps in writing, and keep me posted. We will touch base again next Monday.

Every Monday morning I read about twenty updates from regional managers in Latin America, Europe and Asia. I read most of them on my phone, between two meetings, so I have about one minute for each one. The good updates all look the same. The first line tells me if the project is on track or behind schedule. Then I get one or two highlights, not a diary of the whole week. After that comes the part most managers hide at the end: the blocker. If something is stopping your work, flag it early, in the first half of the update. I cannot help with a problem that I hear about three weeks later. I also like it when a manager tells me what a client actually said. For example, the doctor said she was happy with our visit. That sentence is much stronger than, the visit went well. And finally, every update needs next steps, with a name and a date. Who is going to do what, and when? If I know that, I do not need a meeting.

My name is Diego, and I manage the commercial team in Mexico. Six months ago my director called me after a monthly review. She told me that my numbers were good, but that my updates were too long. She said she read them on her phone and could not find the important part. I was surprised, because I thought a long update showed that I was working hard. So I asked her what she wanted. She said she wanted three things: the status, the problem, and the next step. The following week I sent her five lines. She replied in two minutes. She said it was the best update I had ever sent her. Later, a colleague from Spain told me that her director had said the same thing to her. Now I report what clients tell me in one sentence, I flag problems on the first day, and I never send an update without an action item. My updates are shorter, and my director answers them faster.

The Porto Alegre project is on track this week. The highlight: Doctor Costa said she was happy with our joint visit. I want to flag one blocker: the distributor told me the November shipment would arrive two weeks late. Next steps: I will call the supply team today and report back by Friday.
